page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.mn4.2xlarge is a general-purpose virtual machine belonging to the shared resource instance class. The configuration supplies 8 shared vCPUs across 4 physical cores via hyper-threading on an Intel Xeon 8163 processor operating at 2.5 GHz. Compute features include 33 MB of L3 cache alongside support for AVX and AVX-512 extensions. The server is allocated 32.0 GB of system memory, matching a standard 1:4 vCPU-to-RAM ratio. No local disk storage or hardware accelerators are bundled with the instance, requiring reliance on remote block storage, while baseline network throughput is rated at 1 Gbps.

Benchmark results demonstrate a clear bifurcation between single-threaded efficiency and parallel capacity. Single-core evaluations reflect aged execution pipelines, with Geekbench single-core reaching 908.0 and gzip compression reporting 18.97 GB/sec, placing them in the lower quartile of modern virtual hosts. In contrast, multi-threaded tasks demonstrate mid-tier stability; PassMark CPU scores reach 9097.87 and Geekbench multi-core registers 4765.0. Memory throughput remains balanced, sustaining 60.23 GB/sec on uncached read blocks and supporting 9.31 million Redis SET operations per second, though database test operations score on the lower spectrum.

Because the vCPU allocation relies on shared physical host resources, processing performance can exhibit variability during peak hypervisor contention. This architectural tradeoff yields favorable resource density for scenarios that do not demand sustained, unthrottled computing power. Workloads aligned with the profile of the ecs.mn4.2xlarge include staging and test platforms, build nodes, continuous integration pipelines, background queuing workers, and low-traffic internal line-of-business applications.

Benchmark outcomes reveal modest single-thread metrics, including lower Geekbench and compression throughput, alongside mid-range multi-core performance in stress-ng and PassMark evaluations. The shared CPU profile makes this instance a practical resource-dense allocation for development servers, continuous integration tasks, internal business tools, and intermediate queuing services that do not require dedicated core cycles.
